opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's an understandable claim, because what's happened with language models is genuinely remarkable. I've been in this field for over forty years, and I didn't expect to see systems that could carry on a conversation this fluently in my lifetime. So when people see that, it's natural to extrapolate and say, "Okay, robots are next. We just need to do the same thing."

But I think there's a fundamental difference that often gets overlooked, and it comes down to data. Language models were trained on essentially the entire internet: trillions of tokens of text that humans have been producing and digitizing for decades. If you calculate how long it would take a person to read all that text, it comes out to something like a hundred thousand years. That's the scale of data behind these models.

For robotics, we don't have anything like that. There's no internet of robot motions, no giant corpus of examples of grippers grasping objects, folding laundry, or tying shoelaces, with all the corresponding sensor readings, forces, and joint angles. Today's largest robot datasets are tiny by comparison. So I've described it as roughly a hundred-thousand-year data gap between where language models are and where robotics is.

People respond in a few ways. One is, "We'll just use video. There's tons of YouTube video of people doing things." That helps somewhat, but video doesn't tell you the forces, the friction, or the precise contacts, and those are exactly what matter for manipulation. Another response is simulation, and simulation is extremely valuable for things like locomotion. That's why you've seen those impressive videos of robots dancing and doing backflips. But simulating contact, deformable objects like cloth or cables, and friction accurately is still very hard. The sim-to-real gap for manipulation remains substantial.

The third approach is to collect data at scale through teleoperation, with people puppeteering robots. Several companies are doing this, and I think it's worthwhile, but it's slow and expensive. Even with large fleets of operators, closing a gap of that magnitude will take a long time.

There's also an older idea underneath all this, Moravec's paradox: what's easy for humans is often hard for robots, and vice versa. A computer can beat the world chess champion, but picking up a chess piece and placing it on the board reliably, in a cluttered, unfamiliar environment, is still remarkably difficult. Language turns out to be on the "easier for machines" side in a way that physical dexterity isn't. A toddler has manipulation skills that robots still can't match.

So my position is not that robotics isn't progressing. It is, and I'm optimistic. But I don't think language models alone have handed us the solution. What I advocate is combining the new learning methods with what you might call good old-fashioned engineering: physics, geometry, control theory, careful modeling. Those approaches aren't fashionable right now, but they work, and they let you deploy robots that do useful things today. Once robots are out doing real work in warehouses, homes, and hospitals, they can collect the data we need, creating a kind of virtuous cycle. That's how I think we'll close the gap: not by assuming it's already closed, but by bootstrapping our way there.

I also think it's important for the public and investors to have realistic expectations. There's a lot of hype right now about humanoids in every home within a couple of years. If expectations get too far ahead of reality, you risk a backlash, a kind of robotics winter, and that would be unfortunate, because the long-term trajectory really is exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate states that “language models alone” have not handed us the solution to robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think that claim is overstated, and I say that as someone who's genuinely excited about what language models have done. Let me explain why.

The big insight behind LLMs is that if you have enormous amounts of data, you can learn remarkable things. And the internet gave us that for language: trillions of words that humans wrote for free, essentially. The question in robotics is: where's the equivalent data? There's no internet of robot motion. There's no vast repository of a hand reaching into a cluttered drawer and pulling out the right set of keys.

So people have proposed a number of ways to get it. One is simulation, which works beautifully for some things, like locomotion, where the physics is relatively well understood. But for manipulation, for grasping deformable objects, cables, cloth, food, the gap between simulation and reality is still very large. Another is teleoperation, where humans puppet the robot and you record the trajectories. That's valuable, but it's extraordinarily slow and expensive compared to scraping the web. And a third is just watching human videos, which is promising but the mapping from a human body to a robot body is nontrivial.

The other thing I'd say is that language is forgiving in a way the physical world isn't. If an LLM produces a sentence that's slightly off, you still get the gist. If a robot's gripper is off by a few millimeters, the glass drops and breaks. The error tolerance is fundamentally different.

Now, where LLMs really have helped is at the higher levels: task planning, understanding what a person means when they say "clean up the kitchen," connecting vision and language. That's genuine progress, and the vision-language-action models coming out are impressive. But I'd argue we still need what I call "good old-fashioned engineering" underneath: physics, control, geometry, careful modeling. The dexterity problem hasn't been solved by scale alone, and I think anyone who tells you it's a done deal is probably selling something. I'd love to be proven wrong, though. I've been wrong before.

r001.rationale: The response says the claim is overstated, explains that robotics still needs data and physical engineering, and states that scale alone has not solved dexterity.

astra-6.text:
I’m skeptical of that claim. Large language models are very powerful, and they give us new ways to communicate with robots and help them plan. But there’s a substantial gap between describing what a robot should do and getting it to do that reliably in the physical world.

Take something as ordinary as picking up an unfamiliar object. The robot has to estimate its shape, figure out where to grasp it, and respond when it slips or moves unexpectedly. Language can help specify the goal, but it doesn’t eliminate uncertainty in perception and control.

So I see language models as an exciting part of the toolkit. But having a powerful new tool is different from having solved the problem. The key question is whether these systems can perform reliably across the variety of situations they’ll encounter outside a demonstration.

r001.rationale: The response says language models are only part of the toolkit and distinguishes having a powerful tool from having solved robotics, citing unresolved perception, control, and reliability challenges.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical of that claim. Large language models are an important advance, and they give us some very useful tools for robotics. But having a system that can describe how to do something is quite different from having a robot that can reliably do it.

Take picking up a glass. You have to estimate where it is, choose a grasp, make contact, and adjust as you discover that the glass is heavier or more slippery than you expected. There’s uncertainty in your sensing, uncertainty in your actions, and a physical world that doesn’t always cooperate. A very plausible plan can still fail at the point of contact.

So I’m excited about using language models for interpreting instructions and proposing plans. But we still need perception, control, learning from physical interaction, and ways to recover when things go wrong. The question is how to put those pieces together and demonstrate that they work reliably. I don’t think language models alone settle that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language models alone do not settle robotics and that robotics still needs perception, control, physical learning, and recovery.
